Vignette:
Ravi had spent the autumn of 1969 learning that the jungle did not warn you before it took you. He remembered the way the damp air clung to his uniform, the sudden rupture of rifle fire that split the canopy, and the choking cloud of cordite that followed the screams. One moment he was checking his ammunition; the next, the earth was rising to meet him, dirt and crushed leaves filling his mouth, his chest heaving as he waited for the silence that never fully came. Years later, he could still hear the specific cadence of those shots, but more than the sound, it was the sudden vacuum of air that preceded the firing, the way the birds had gone quiet just seconds before the first burst, that had lodged itself behind his ribs. He had come to believe that the world operated on unpredictable thresholds, and that safety was an illusion maintained only by constant readiness. In the decades that followed, Ravi’s routine narrowed to manage the weight of that conviction. He avoided the downtown district where delivery trucks backed up with sharp, metallic clangs, and he stopped attending his sister’s Diwali gatherings because the sudden burst of firecrackers made his hands tremble so badly he could not hold his tea. At the warehouse where he had spent thirty years organizing freight, he learned to position his chair near the loading dock door, never with his back to the corridor. When a pallet jack squeaked across the concrete one Tuesday, he was on the floor before the foreman finished shouting, his breath coming in short, sharp pulls, his eyes locked on the ventilation grate as if it might open onto another jungle floor. He told himself he was just protecting his knees from the hard ground, but staying near the exit gave him a fragile sense of control. The high shelves and echoing aisles made his chest feel too tight, and stepping away from them felt necessary. The accumulation of these choices ran parallel to the quiet changes in his personal life. He stopped answering calls from old friends who asked about his health, fearing they would hear the tightness in his voice. He took longer routes to the grocery store, turning away from construction sites and subway entrances, convinced it was simply easier to avoid the crowds. His ex-wife had eventually moved on, and he had accepted the distance, certain that his sudden withdrawals and the way he sometimes stared through people made shared routines impossible. He no longer attended Veterans of Foreign Wars meetings because the shared stories of deployment made his jaw ache with the effort of sitting still. At seventy-nine, the strain finally outpaced his ability to manage it. The recent onset of waking three hours before dawn, heart hammering against his ribs, and the way he now flinched when the microwave beeped at home made it impossible to ignore the mounting fatigue. What brought him to the clinic was a Tuesday morning at the warehouse when a forklift reversed with a loud, rhythmic beeping. He had dropped a clipboard, stepped into the narrow gap between two shelving units, and stood perfectly still until a junior associate tapped his shoulder. The touch had sent a shock through him, and he realized his hands were shaking uncontrollably. He had come to the appointment hoping to stop the exhaustion that was making it difficult to walk up the stairs to his apartment, though what frightened him most was the quiet certainty that he might never feel safe in his own skin again. He was ready to try something that did not require him to keep watch.
